claims.text: The proposed intervention is to replace continuous-wave laser processing with pulsed laser processing during additive manufacturing of cobalt-free AlCrFeNiSi.
Pulsed laser processing uses short, high-intensity energy bursts.
Discrete, controlled laser-energy bursts refine melt-pool dynamics.
Discrete laser-energy bursts minimize heat accumulation.
Pulsed laser processing reduces thermal gradients during melting and solidification relative to continuous-wave processing.
Reduced thermal gradients produce a more homogeneous AlCrFeNiSi microstructure.
Reduced thermal gradients reduce elemental segregation in additively manufactured AlCrFeNiSi.
Reduced thermal gradients lower residual stress in additively manufactured AlCrFeNiSi.
Reduced thermal gradients result in fewer manufacturing defects.
Pulsed laser processing improves the mechanical integrity of AlCrFeNiSi relative to continuous-wave laser processing.
Pulsed laser processing increases tensile strength relative to continuous-wave processing.
Pulsed laser processing improves ductility relative to continuous-wave processing.
The hypothesis is applicable in standard laser powder bed fusion equipment operated at ambient pressure with typical powder preparation and post-processing protocols.
The magnitude of mechanical-property improvement depends on laser parameters and processing conditions.
A controlled comparison using identical powder can test pulsed processing against continuous-wave processing through microscopy, EDS, residual-stress measurements, and mechanical tests.
The hypothesis is falsified if pulsed samples show no statistically significant reductions in segregation and residual stress and no measurable improvement in mechanical integrity.
